{
  "anomaly_detected": true,
  "confidence": 0.85,
  "anomalies": [
    {
      "category": "wrong_value",
      "components": ["R7"],
      "pins": ["R7.1", "R7.2", "J12.B5"],
      "nets": ["Net-(J12-CC2)", "GND"],
      "observed": "R7 is the CC2 pull-down on the USB-C receptacle, but its value is 5.1M (5.1 MΩ). Its partner R1, on the CC1 line, is 5.1k. The two CC pull-downs are therefore mismatched by a factor of 1000.",
      "expected": "Both CC1 and CC2 pull-downs should be 5.1 kΩ (R1 is 5.1k). The spec says the CC pins go through R1/R7 at 5.1 kΩ each to declare a default-current USB-C sink.",
      "evidence": [
        {"source": "netlist", "quote": "(comp (ref \"R7\") (value \"5.1M\")"},
        {"source": "netlist", "quote": "(comp (ref \"R1\") (value \"5.1k\")"},
        {"source": "netlist", "quote": "(net (code \"25\") (name \"Net-(J12-CC2)\") (class \"Default\") (node (ref \"J12\") (pin \"B5\") (pinfunction \"CC2\") (pintype \"bidirectional\")) (node (ref \"R7\") (pin \"2\") (pintype \"passive\")))"},
        {"source": "spec", "quote": "USB-C CC1/CC2 pins go through `R1`/`R7` (5.1 kΩ each) to `GND`"},
        {"source": "spice", "quote": "R7 0 Net-_J12-CC2_ 5.1Meg"}
      ],
      "impact": "The CC2 pin is effectively floating rather than pulled down. The USB-C source cannot reliably detect the sink or its orientation, so a standard USB-C supply may not enable VBUS or may use the wrong orientation. This can break USB power and programming when plugged in with CC2 as the active line.",
      "confidence": 0.85
    },
    {
      "category": "extra_component",
      "components": ["J5"],
      "pins": ["J5.1", "J5.2"],
      "nets": ["/Microcontroller/HEATER", "GND"],
      "observed": "A second 2-position screw terminal, J5, sits on the heater control net. Pin 2 is on /Microcontroller/HEATER (GPIO1, which also drives U6 IN and DIAG_EN) and pin 1 is on GND. The spec documents only J6 as the heater connector and does not mention J5.",
      "expected": "The spec describes a single heater output through the TPS1H200AQDGNRQ1 to connector J6. A direct GPIO-driven terminal to GND is not described.",
      "evidence": [
        {"source": "netlist", "quote": "(net (code \"4\") (name \"/Microcontroller/HEATER\") (class \"Default\") (node (ref \"D2\") (pin \"2\") (pinfunction \"A\") (pintype \"passive\")) (node (ref \"J5\") (pin \"2\") (pinfunction \"Pin_2\") (pintype \"passive\"))"},
        {"source": "spec", "quote": "Drives a single **heater output** net through a smart high-side switch (`U6`, TPS1H200AQDGNRQ1)"}
      ],
      "impact": "If connected to a load, J5 would bypass the high-side switch and its current limit and fault protection and drive a load directly from a GPIO pin. The heater could then be energised without the protected path. Its purpose is unclear from the files.",
      "confidence": 0.3
    }
  ],
  "summary": "R7, the CC2 pull-down on the USB-C receptacle, is 5.1 MΩ where the spec and its mirror R1 call for 5.1 kΩ, which defeats USB-C sink detection. The unexplained J5 terminal on the heater GPIO net is a lower-confidence second candidate."
}

anomalies.observed: R7 is the CC2 pull-down on the USB-C receptacle, but its value is 5.1M (5.1 MΩ). Its partner R1, on the CC1 line, is 5.1k. The two CC pull-downs are therefore mismatched by a factor of 1000.
anomalies.expected: Both CC1 and CC2 pull-downs should be 5.1 kΩ (R1 is 5.1k). The spec says the CC pins go through R1/R7 at 5.1 kΩ each to declare a default-current USB-C sink.

evidence.quote: USB-C CC1/CC2 pins go through `R1`/`R7` (5.1 kΩ each) to `GND`

anomalies.impact: The CC2 pin is effectively floating rather than pulled down. The USB-C source cannot reliably detect the sink or its orientation, so a standard USB-C supply may not enable VBUS or may use the wrong orientation. This can break USB power and programming when plugged in with CC2 as the active line.

anomalies.observed: A second 2-position screw terminal, J5, sits on the heater control net. Pin 2 is on /Microcontroller/HEATER (GPIO1, which also drives U6 IN and DIAG_EN) and pin 1 is on GND. The spec documents only J6 as the heater connector and does not mention J5.
anomalies.expected: The spec describes a single heater output through the TPS1H200AQDGNRQ1 to connector J6. A direct GPIO-driven terminal to GND is not described.

evidence.quote: Drives a single **heater output** net through a smart high-side switch (`U6`, TPS1H200AQDGNRQ1)

anomalies.impact: If connected to a load, J5 would bypass the high-side switch and its current limit and fault protection and drive a load directly from a GPIO pin. The heater could then be energised without the protected path. Its purpose is unclear from the files.
